title: I See Your Tears Hold Back, Patience Your Nature
intro: The heading in Ibn Khalawayh's recension says that Abu Firas composed it as a boast when he heard that the Byzantines were saying they had never taken a prisoner without stripping him of his weapons, except Abu Firas. His editor Sami al-Dahhan places it in his Byzantine captivity, 351–355 AH (962–966 CE), which makes it one of the Rumiyyat, and al-Tha'alibi quotes it among his prison poems. It opens with twenty-five lines of love: a man who hides his passion by day and weeps at night, a beloved who pretends not to know him, a frightened gazelle that shies and comes back. With “Do not pretend not to know me, cousin” it turns to boasting: the armies he has led, his generosity, his restraint with the women of the defeated, the battle in which he chose capture over flight, and the glory of his people. Al-Dahhan calls it “almost the best known of all Abu Firas's poems”, and two of its phrases are still everyday Arabic: a modern dictionary gives “two things, the sweeter of them bitter” and “on a dark night the full moon is missed” among its examples.

translation: I see your tears hold back; patience is your nature.
Has love no say over you, to forbid or command?
1.sharh: Someone, or the poet himself, remarks that he never weeps and seems wholly ruled by patience, as if love had no power to order him about. The question sets up the confession that follows.

translation: Yes, I long, and I burn inside,
but a man like me does not let his secret out.
2.sharh: He admits the longing and the ache of love, but his rank forbids him to show them. A prince and a warrior keeps his weakness to himself.

translation: When night takes me in, I give love free rein
and humble a tear whose nature is pride.
3.sharh: Alone at night he lets passion have its way and weeps. His tears are proud by nature and refuse to flow, so making them fall is a kind of humbling. He is patient in public and weeps in private.

translation: The fire between my ribs all but shines out
when longing and brooding fan it.
4.sharh: The love he hides burns so fiercely that its light almost shows through his chest whenever desire and thoughts of her stir it up.

translation: You who soothe me with hopes of union, while death comes first:
if I die of thirst, let no rain fall.
5.sharh: She keeps promising to meet him, but death will reach him before she keeps her word. If he dies thirsting for her, rain afterwards is worth nothing to him: union after death is no union.

translation: I kept the love between us, and you let it go;
and better than some loyalty is an excuse for you.
6.sharh: He kept faith while she squandered their love, yet he still finds excuses for her, and holds that forgiving her is finer than a loyalty that keeps accounts.

translation: These days are nothing but pages
whose letters the hand that wrote them scrapes away.
7.sharh: Time writes the story of people's lives and then erases what it wrote. Nothing written on the days lasts, neither love nor promise.

translation: My life for a young woman among those leaving the camp at dawn:
my love for her is a sin, and her beauty its excuse.
8.sharh: He offers his life for a girl of the departing tribe. People blame him for loving her, but anyone who saw her would forgive him.

translation: She leans towards those who slander me,
but my ear is deaf to anyone who slanders her.
9.sharh: She listens readily to gossip against him, while he will not hear a word against her. She believes what she is told about him; he believes nothing told about her.

translation: I went to live in the desert while my people stayed settled, because
I think any home you are not part of a wasteland.
10.sharh: He left his settled family and followed her into the desert, because any place without her feels empty to him, however many people live there.

translation: I fought my own people for love of you, though they and I,
but for your love, would be water and wine.
11.sharh: His love set him against his own clan, though without it they would be as close as water mixed with wine. Love alone divided him from the people nearest to him.

translation: And if what the slanderers said were so, and it was not,
faith can tear down what unbelief has built.
12.sharh: Even if the slanderers' charge against him were true, which it is not, his faithfulness since would wipe it out, as faith undoes what came before it. It recalls the Prophet's saying that Islam demolishes what came before it, and some manuscripts read “Islam” here.

translation: I kept faith, and some faithfulness is humiliation,
with a gentle girl of the camp whose nature is betrayal.
13.sharh: He stayed true to a charming girl who is faithless by nature. He knows that loyalty to someone who betrays you is degrading, and keeps it all the same.

translation: Sedate, yet the first flush of youth stirs her,
and at times she frisks as a colt frisks.
14.sharh: She is composed and dignified, but she is young, and now and then her youth gets the better of her and she turns playful, like a young horse kicking up its heels.

translation: She asks me, “Who are you?”, though she knows full well.
Can a young man like me, as I am, go unknown?
15.sharh: She pretends not to recognise him, out of coquetry, though she knows him perfectly well. He is too well known, and too plainly in love, to be a stranger to anyone.

translation: I answered as she wished, and as love wished for her:
“Your victim.” She said, “Which one? There are so many.”
16.sharh: He gives the answer she wants to hear: he is the man her love has killed. She cuts him down by asking which one, since love of her has killed so many.

translation: I told her, “If you wished, you would not torment me
with questions about me when you know all about me.”
17.sharh: He protests that her questions are meant only to torment him. She has no need to ask: she knows everything about him, inside and out.

translation: She said, “Time has brought you low since we parted.”
I said, “God forbid. It was you, not time.”
18.sharh: She remarks that the years since their parting have worn him down. He answers that it was not time that wasted him but her, her love and her coldness.

translation: Sorrow would have had no road to the heart but for you;
love is the bridge that ruin crosses.
19.sharh: Without her, grief could never have reached his heart. Love opened the way: it is a bridge over which decay and sorrow came in, so he blames love, not fate, for his ruin.

translation: And a life is lost between jest and earnest:
when parting spares it, brooding torments it.
20.sharh: He is worn away by not knowing whether she is joking or serious. Even when they are not apart, thinking about her gives him no peace, so near or far he suffers. Al-Dahhan's text has “coldness” for “brooding”.

translation: So I knew that after me no lover would keep his pride,
and that my hand held nothing of what it had clung to.
21.sharh: If a man as proud as he could be humbled by love, no lover after him can hope to keep his dignity. And for all his clinging, he has come away empty-handed.

translation: I turned my case over and found no rest:
when one care made me forget, her coldness pressed on me.
22.sharh: He looks at his plight from every side and sees no relief. Whenever some other worry takes his mind off her, her neglect comes back and torments him again.

translation: So I gave in to the rule of time and to hers:
the fault is hers, unpunished, and I am the one in the right.
23.sharh: He submits to fate and to her. She is to blame and pays nothing for it; he is blameless, and still he accepts whatever she decides.

translation: It is as if I were calling, across a broad gully, a gazelle
on a rise, dark-lipped, wrapped in fear,
24.sharh: He compares his courtship to calling a frightened gazelle that stands on high ground, too afraid to trust the voice calling her. The comparison runs on into the next line.

translation: who shies one moment and comes near the next, as if
calling a fawn in the valley that cannot run fast enough.
25.sharh: The gazelle bolts, then turns back, torn between flight and the fawn that cannot keep up with her. The beloved is the same, pulling away and then drawing near.

translation: Do not pretend not to know me, cousin: the man
you pretend not to know is known in desert and town.
26.sharh: He tells her to stop feigning ignorance of him, since everyone, nomad and settled, knows who he is. With this line the poem turns from love to boasting.

translation: Do not pretend not to know me: I am no stranger
when feet slip and men pray for victory.
27.sharh: In the worst of a battle, when men give way and call on God for victory, everyone knows who he is. That is where his worth shows.

translation: I lead every battalion
so used to victory that victory never leaves it.
28.sharh: He commands great armies, and every troop he leads is so used to winning that victory never deserts it. In his telling, victory is not luck but the habit of his men.

translation: I am quick to dismount in every place of fear,
where many a sidelong glare falls on those who dismount.
29.sharh: Time and again he leaves the saddle to meet the enemy on foot in the most dangerous places, where every man who does so draws furious looks from the other side.

translation: I go thirsty till swords and spears have drunk,
and hungry till the wolf and the vulture are full.
30.sharh: He forgets his own thirst and hunger in battle until his weapons have drunk the enemy's blood and the scavengers have fed on the dead.

translation: I do not fall at dawn on a camp whose men are away,
nor on an army until my warnings have reached it first.
31.sharh: Dawn was the hour for raids, but he will not fall on a camp whose fighting men are absent, nor attack an army that has had no warning. He takes no enemy unawares and sees no glory in beating the helpless.

translation: Many a strong house that did not fear me
I came upon with death, I and the dawn together.
32.sharh: Strongholds whose people felt safe from him saw him arrive at first light, bringing death as the sun came up. Dawn was the usual hour for a raid, and he rises over them together with it.

translation: Many a camp I drove my horses at until I held it,
routed, and the veils and head-cloths turned me back.
33.sharh: He charged camps and took them, but when he saw the veiled women his sense of honour held him back, and he did not take them captive.

translation: Many a woman trailing her skirts came towards me,
and found in me no scowl and no harshness.
34.sharh: A woman of rank came to him after the battle, and he met her with gentleness, not the grim face of a conqueror.

translation: I gave her everything my army had taken
and left without one veil of her clothes lifted.
35.sharh: He handed her all his army's spoils and went away without exposing her in the least, guarding her honour. Some manuscripts have “her tents” for “her clothes”.

translation: Wealth has never made me proud with its fine robes,
nor has poverty spent a night keeping me from generosity.
36.sharh: Riches never made him arrogant and want never made him mean, not even for a night. Wealth is pictured as a man parading in fine clothes.

translation: What need have I of money, to seek its increase?
If I do not keep my honour whole, let wealth not grow.
37.sharh: He does not chase riches for their own sake. Money is only for protecting his honour; if it fails at that, he wishes it no increase.

translation: I was taken, though my men were not unarmed in battle,
my horse was no colt, and its rider no novice.
38.sharh: He turns to his capture. It was no fault of his companions, his horse or himself: they were armed, the horse seasoned, the rider experienced.

translation: But when fate is decreed for a man,
neither land nor sea will shield him.
39.sharh: When fate has decided something for a man there is no escaping it, whether he runs by land or by sea. His capture was destiny, not failure.

translation: My comrades said, “Flight, or death?”
I said, “Two things, the sweeter of them bitter.”
40.sharh: In the battle his companions offered him the choice of running or dying. Both were hateful to him: flight meant disgrace, death meant the end.

translation: But I go on towards what brings me no shame,
and enough said of two courses when the better is captivity.
41.sharh: He took the course that carried no dishonour: he neither fled nor threw his life away, and accepted capture as the better of two evils. That captivity was the better says enough about the choice.

translation: They say to me, “You sold safety for death.”
I said, “By God, I lost nothing.”
42.sharh: People reproach him for standing his ground when he could have saved himself. He swears that he lost nothing, because he kept his honour.

translation: Will death keep away from me for an hour
if captivity and harm keep away?
43.sharh: Death will come whatever he does; escaping capture would not have kept it away for an hour. So there was no sense in buying safety with flight.

translation: It is death, so choose what raises your name;
a man does not die while his name lives.
44.sharh: Since death is certain, a man should choose the course that makes his name last. As long as he is remembered, he is not truly dead.

translation: They count it a favour that they left me my clothes, but
I was wearing clothes red with their blood.
45.sharh: The Byzantines make much of having left him his clothes instead of stripping him like other prisoners. That was no kindness: his clothes were soaked in their blood. This answers the boast reported in the poem's heading.

translation: And my sword's hilt: its blade snapped in them;
my spear's butt: its upper shaft smashed in them.
46.sharh: He fought until his weapons broke: his sword blade snapped off at the hilt and his spear shattered down to its butt. He was taken only when he had nothing left to fight with.

translation: My people will remember me when things grow grave:
on a dark night the full moon is missed.
47.sharh: When his people face real danger they will miss him, as the moon is missed most on the darkest night. Al-Dahhan attributes the second half to Antara.

translation: If I live, then the spearing they know,
those spears and swords, and the lean chestnut horses.
48.sharh: If he survives captivity he will go back to the life his people know him for, spear and sword and the warhorse. Prison will not change him.

translation: If I die, a man must die,
however long his days, however wide his life.
49.sharh: If he dies a prisoner, that is the end every man comes to, however long he lives, and he will not fear it. With the line before, he sets out the only two outcomes he allows.

translation: Had another filled the gap I filled, they would have been content with him;
gold would not be dear if brass found buyers.
50.sharh: His people need him because no one else can take his place. Gold fetches a high price only because no one will take brass in its place.

translation: We are a people with no middle ground:
ours the first place above the world, or the grave.
51.sharh: His clan will not settle for a modest place: either they stand at the head of all mankind or they die. The rhyme sets the two words against each other, sadr, the first place, and qabr, the grave.

translation: Our lives are cheap to us in the pursuit of glory;
whoever seeks a beautiful bride does not find the dowry too high.
52.sharh: They spend their lives freely for honour. Glory is the beautiful bride, and their lives are the bride-price, which no true suitor thinks too steep.

translation: The mightiest of this world's children, the highest of the high,
the noblest of all who walk the earth, and no boast.
53.sharh: He ends by praising his people as the mightiest, loftiest and most generous on earth, and then disclaims boasting, in a phrase that makes the boast complete.

3.1.3.head: أَضوى
3.1.3.meaning: Brought me in, gave me shelter: the dictionaries cite “the night brought him in to us”. Al-Duwayhi glosses it “weakened me”.

3.1.4-6.meaning: “I stretch out love's hand”: I give love free rein.

4.1.5.head: جَوانِح
4.1.5.meaning: The ribs over the chest, and so the breast.

5.1.1.head: مُعَلِّلَة
5.1.1.meaning: “She who soothes me”: she keeps him hoping with promises, as a child is soothed with something to keep it quiet.

7.2.5.head: بَشر
7.2.5.meaning: Bashr: scraping the face off a hide; here, erasing.

8.1.1.meaning: “With my soul”: I would ransom her with my life.

10.1.1.head: بَدا
10.1.1.meaning: Went out to live in the desert.

11.2.4-5.meaning: Water and wine: two things that mix so well they cannot be told apart.

12.2.6.head: الكُفر
12.2.6.meaning: Kufr: unbelief, denying God; at root, covering and denying a gift.

13.2.1.head: آنِسَة
13.2.1.meaning: Anisa: a young woman of gentle, friendly temper, good company.

17.1.6.head: تَعَنَّتَ
17.1.6.meaning: To press someone with questions meant to trouble or trap him.

24.1.4.head: مَيثاء
24.1.4.meaning: Maytha': soft, level ground; also a broad gully that opens into a valley.

24.2.3.head: ظَمياء
24.2.3.meaning: Zamya': with dark lips, a beauty in a gazelle and in a woman.

26.1.3-5.meaning: “Daughter of my uncle”: how a man addressed a woman of his own clan, and a beloved.

27.2.2-3.meaning: “Feet slip”: when men give way in the press of battle.

27.2.5.head: النَّضر
27.2.5.meaning: Nadr: so the reciter says it, as al-Duwayhi's edition prints it; nadr is gold, which makes no sense here. Ibn Khalawayh's recension in al-Dahhan's edition has nasr, victory, and the translation and commentary follow it.

28.1.2.head: جَرّار
28.1.2.meaning: Jarrar: “one who drags”, a man who leads an army a thousand strong.

29.1.2.head: نَزّال
29.1.2.meaning: One who often dismounts to fight on foot where it is most dangerous.

29.2.4-5.meaning: A sidelong look from the corner of the eye, in anger.

31.1.4.head: الخَلوف
31.1.4.meaning: Khaluf: a camp whose men are away, leaving the women and the weak.

34.1.1-2.meaning: “Trailing her skirts”: a free woman of rank in long gowns.

40.2.4-5.meaning: “The sweeter of the two is bitter”: it became a proverb for a choice between two evils.

46.2.5.head: الصَّدر
46.2.5.meaning: The upper part of a spear, below the head.

48.2.4.head: الضُّمَّر
48.2.4.meaning: Lean horses, trained down for racing and war.

48.2.5.head: الشُّقر
48.2.5.meaning: Chestnuts: horses of a clear red.

53.2.5-6.meaning: “And no boast”: the words of the Prophet's saying “I am the master of the children of Adam, and no boast”.
